key_insight: The paper turns short-range-order alloy design into a differentiable optimization problem, enabling direct gradient-based search from target SRO to target mechanical property.
engineering_relevance: This provides a faster, scalable route for designing multi-principal-element alloys with property targets, reducing reliance on trial-and-error reverse Monte Carlo workflows.
method: Replace random-swap reverse Monte Carlo with continuous atom-occupancy optimization using gradient descent.
Add a physics-based thermodynamic correction so designed SRO remains realistic for multi-element alloys.
Train a small neural network to predict mechanical properties from composition and SRO statistics, closing the design loop.
evidence_signal: Across nine FCC and BCC alloys, the pipeline reproduced SRO-driven stiffness changes from -20% to +57%, and on a Co-Cr-Ni benchmark matched three of four target stiffness values within 6%.
watch_item: The method depends on sufficiently large supercells for reliable trends; the paper notes that 108-atom cells can mislead and that at least 864 atoms were needed for correct stiffness direction and magnitude.
paper_title: Differentiable inverse design of short-range order in high-entropy alloys: from target sro to target property
